text: A model can only learn from the columns you hand it. Raw columns are often not the most useful form of the information — a timestamp is just a huge number to an algorithm, a total is meaningless without the item count. Feature engineering turns raw columns into inputs that make the pattern easier to learn, and it's often the highest-return work in a whole project. You already have the tools — it's mostly pandas.

Imagine four retail orders with an order date, a total, an item count, and the customer's annual income. A date is one column but hides many signals — the month for seasonality, the day of the week, whether it falls on a weekend. Pandas exposes these through the dot dt accessor: df order_date dot dt dot month, and dayofweek greater than or equal to 5 for weekends.

Two columns often say more together than apart. Order total divided by item count gives the average item price, a customer-behavior signal neither column shows alone. Other common ratios: time since last purchase, debt-to-income, clicks per visit.
Income is right-skewed — a few very large values stretch the scale. A log transform compresses that tail. np dot log1p computes log of 1 plus x, which stays safe even when a value can be zero.

Sometimes the band matters more than the exact number. pd dot cut turns a continuous column into categories — here, low, mid, and high income bands. Binning throws information away, so use it when you have a real reason to believe thresholds matter, and remember a new categorical column then needs encoding, exactly like you saw earlier in this chapter.

Running all five new columns on our four orders: row 1 is a Saturday, which is why is_weekend comes out True there. Average item price ranges from 30 to 50 dollars across the orders, log income ranges from 10.37 to 12.43, and the income bands split cleanly into low, mid, high, and mid.

Three guardrails apply every time. Only use information available at prediction time — a feature like total refunds this year, computed after the fact, would leak the future, exactly the problem from the data leakage lesson. Compute learned quantities on the training set only — simple row-wise ratios are safe, but anything using a statistic across rows, like a mean or a bin edge, must be fit on the training split.

And test whether it actually helped — a new feature is a hypothesis. Compare validation performance with and without it, and keep it only if it earns its place. To recap: split dates, combine columns into ratios, tame skew with logs, and bin when bands genuinely matter. Guard against leakage, and let validation scores decide what to keep. Next, since you can now create many features, you need a way to choose among them: feature selection.
